title: Al-Muzzammil, whole
hook: the night prayer and measured recitation (Surah 73)
tomorrow: why would anyone feed a stranger and refuse a thank-you?

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Mulk: the surah read before sleep, asking you to look at the sky again, and again. Look again. Tonight, someone is told to get up instead.

The hoodie pulled all the way over the head, the blanket over the face: the oldest way to tell the world, not now. There's a story with a blanket in it. A man comes home from a cave on a mountain, his heart pounding. Sahih al-Bukhari records what he says to his wife, Khadijah: cover me, cover me. She wraps him up and stays with him until the fear leaves. The man is the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and something has just spoken to him in that cave. A surah of the Qur'an opens by calling him exactly that: the wrapped one. You'd expect the next word to be rest. It isn't.
screen: `THE BLANKET OVER THE HEAD.` → `COVER ME, COVER ME.` → `THE WRAPPED ONE.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's words, it opens: "O thou wrapped up in thy raiment!" And then, instead of rest: rise. Stand in the night, all of it but a little, half, or a bit less, or a bit more, "and chant the Qur'an in measured form." The Arabic word for that is tartil: slow, even, each word given its own place. Not a cram. Not a scroll. Then the surah gives a reason, and it's the detail to tell a friend tonight. It says the hours of the night leave a deeper mark, and words said then come out straighter. Anyone who has typed a message at two in the morning knows the night changes how words land. This surah aims that weight at something worth saying. And here's the turn the story has been waiting for. The surah's last verse comes back to the night and softens it. Your Lord knows you stand nearly two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third. He knows some of you are sick, some traveling to earn a living, some fighting in His cause. So recite what is easy of it. Some commentators hold that this verse came down later than the opening. Either way, the surah keeps both in one place, the call and the mercy. The wrapped one is told to get up. Not forever, and not perfectly. Stand, recite, slowly, as much as is easy.
screen: `WRAPPED UP, TOLD TO RISE.` · `RECITE IN MEASURED FORM.` · `THE NIGHT LEAVES A DEEPER MARK.` · `LATER: RECITE WHAT IS EASY.` · then, large: `STAND, RECITE.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand up where you are, feet steady, hands loose at your sides. Say aloud, slowly, any short line you know by heart, a verse, a surah, or simply a name of God, giving each word its own breath. Then stay standing in the quiet for the rest of the sit.
Al-Muzzammil: the wrapped one. The name of Surah 73, which tells the one under the blanket to rise in the night and recite, slowly.
Keep this one close: stand, recite, only what's easy, and slowly. Al-Muzzammil, read by night.

howItsDone: Muslims who keep a voluntary night prayer (tahajjud or qiyam al-layl) rise after some sleep and recite slowly in it; Surah al-Muzzammil is read as one of its foundations.

Al-Muzzammil.meaning: the wrapped one: the name of Surah 73

Khadijah.meaning: the Prophet's wife, who wrapped him up when he came home

notes: Pickthall 73:1 and 73:4 quoted from memory of the 1930 text; confirm exact wording ('O thou wrapped up in thy raiment!'; 'and chant the Qur'an in measured form').

Paraphrased: the night but a little, half or less or more (73:2–4); the vigil of the night leaving a keener impression and speech more certain (73:6); the last verse, nearly two-thirds, half or a third, the sick, travelers seeking bounty, fighters, 'recite what is easy' (73:20). The counts (two-thirds, half, a third) are the verse's own.

Bukhari 3: the Prophet returns from Hira with his heart beating and says 'cover me' to Khadijah; the script juxtaposes this scene with the surah's address without claiming the surah was revealed at that moment. 'Some commentators hold' that 73:20 came later: confirm the hedge is fair.
